frames.narration: An engineer merges a change to the checkout service. The pipeline builds it once, runs the tests, and stores a signed, immutable artifact called checkout-413 (180 MB) in the registry. This exact file is what will run everywhere.
The engineer starts the deploy. The controller first takes the lock for the checkout service, so no other rollout of it can run, and checks the calendar: no freeze is in force.

Before any host restarts, the artifact is staged. The registry sends checkout-413 to the regional cache tier once, and the hosts download it from the cache ahead of their wave, so installing later is quick.

The first wave is a canary: 20 of the 2,000 hosts, which is 1%. Each is taken out of the load balancer, drained, switched to 413 and put back, and they now serve 1% of real traffic. The version 412 stays on their disk.

The canary bakes for 5 minutes. The health gate compares it with the hosts still on 412 over the same minutes: errors are 0.21% against 0.20%, and the 99th percentile latency is 118 ms against 120 ms. The difference is within noise, so the gate passes.

The controller continues in waves of 200 hosts, 10% of the fleet. Each wave drains, installs, passes a local health check and then the gate before the next one starts. After the third wave, 620 of the 2,000 hosts run 413, and the capacity floor was never broken.
The new checkout screen shipped switched off. Now the engineer turns on its flag for 1% of users, with no deploy. The flag service sends the change to the hosts, and they apply it within seconds.
Errors on the flagged users rise. The engineer flips the kill switch, and the flag is off everywhere in seconds. The code for 413 stays deployed, and no rollback of the fleet was needed.

The last waves pass and all 2,000 hosts run 413. The controller releases the lock and records the deploy: who, which version, and when. Version 412 stays on every disk for a while, so a rollback would be a local switch with nothing to download.
